simulations.title: Application Deployment & Rollback
simulations.goal: Build, tag, deploy a containerised application using a blue-green pipeline and execute a safe rollback when a fault is detected.

learning_content.what: Continuous deployment is the practice of automatically releasing validated software changes to production. Blue-green deployments maintain two identical environments — only one receives live traffic at a time — enabling instant rollbacks without downtime. MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery) is the critical metric: how fast can you restore service when something breaks?
learning_content.how: Follow the pipeline strictly: build → local smoke test → push to registry → trigger deploy → monitor error rate and latency for 5 minutes → confirm healthy. If error rate spikes: rollback first, debug second. Never push an image that failed a smoke test. Document every deployment and every rollback — patterns in deployment failures reveal systemic issues.

sop_steps.instruction: Review the deployment runbook and verify the target environment (staging vs production).
sop_steps.hint: The runbook specifies environment variables, resource limits, and health check endpoints for this deployment.

sop_steps.instruction: Build the Docker container image and tag it with the correct version: `docker build -t app:v2.0.0 .`
sop_steps.hint: Verify the Dockerfile uses the correct base image. Check the build output for any warning messages.

sop_steps.instruction: Run a smoke test on the newly built container locally before pushing to the registry.
sop_steps.hint: Run `docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 app:v2.0.0` and hit the `/health` endpoint to confirm it starts correctly.

sop_steps.instruction: Push the verified image to the central container registry.
sop_steps.hint: Ensure your registry credentials are current. A push failure here means nothing gets deployed.

sop_steps.instruction: Trigger the deployment pipeline and monitor the rollout progress.
sop_steps.hint: Watch the health check status for each new pod — a pod that fails its health check will halt the rolling deployment.

sop_steps.instruction: Verify deployment success by checking application logs and the monitoring dashboard for errors or latency spikes.
sop_steps.hint: Check error rate and p99 latency for 5 minutes post-deploy. A spike in errors is a deployment failure signal.

sop_steps.instruction: If issues are detected, immediately initiate rollback to the last stable version using `kubectl rollout undo`.
sop_steps.hint: Restore service first, investigate second. Rollback first, then debug in a non-production environment.

sop_steps.instruction: Write a deployment incident report detailing what failed, what was rolled back, and next steps.
sop_steps.hint: Include: deployment timestamp, failure symptoms observed, rollback time, and root cause hypothesis.

decision_points.prompt: 5 minutes after deployment, the error rate rises from 0.1% to 8% and customer reports start coming in. What is your immediate action?

options.text: Keep debugging the live code to find a hotfix while users experience errors.
options.consequence: Prolonged outage violates SLA and damages user trust. Always restore service before investigating.

options.text: Immediately execute rollback to v1.9.0 to restore service, then investigate.
options.consequence: Correct. MTTR (Mean Time To Recovery) takes priority. Restore service first, debug in non-prod.

options.text: Shut down all servers to prevent further damage.
options.consequence: Total service shutdown is far worse than the current error rate.

decision_points.prompt: The local smoke test shows the /health endpoint returns a 503 error. Do you push to the registry anyway?

options.text: Yes — it might work fine in the production environment.
options.consequence: A container that fails health checks locally will also fail them in production, causing a deployment outage.

options.text: No — fix the issue and re-run the smoke test before pushing.
options.consequence: Correct. Smoke test failures must be resolved before any artifact is promoted to the registry.

possible_mistakes.description: Failed to rollback a faulty deployment, leaving users experiencing errors.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Prolonged outage, SLA breach, and negative customer impact.

possible_mistakes.description: Deployed the wrong container image tag to production.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Unexpected application state — features may be missing or regressed.

possible_mistakes.description: Pushed an image to the registry despite a failing smoke test.
possible_mistakes.consequence: The broken image will cause a deployment failure or production outage.

possible_mistakes.description: Shut down all servers instead of rolling back.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Self-inflicted total service denial instead of a partial error rate.

hints.text: Rollback command: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<app-name>`.
Check Grafana or Prometheus for the error rate metric. A healthy deployment should show <0.5% error rate.

recommendation_rules.reason: Cybersecurity Incident Response reinforces triage, escalation, and recovery protocols under time pressure.

simulations.title: CNC Machine Setup
simulations.goal: Correctly configure a CNC machine for a new job: workholding, tool setup, offsets, and a safe dry run before production.

learning_content.what: CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machine setup involves loading a workpiece, setting tool offsets, and verifying G-code before production starts. An incorrect setup causes dimensional scrap, broken tooling, or machine crashes — all preventable and expensive. CNC machines follow G-code instructions precisely, so the setup must match the program's assumptions exactly.
learning_content.how: Follow setup in this order: secure the workpiece in the correct orientation → set the Work Coordinate System (G54 origin) → measure and enter each tool's length offset → run a dry-run at reduced feed (10%) with the spindle off → measure the first-off part before committing to a full production run. Never skip the dry run on a new or modified program.

sop_steps.instruction: Review the job traveler / part drawing for required tooling and tolerances.
sop_steps.hint: Check the revision number on the drawing matches the job traveler.

sop_steps.instruction: Mount and secure the correct workholding fixture for this part.
sop_steps.hint: Verify fixture matches the part's datum surfaces shown on the drawing.

sop_steps.instruction: Load the required tools into the correct tool stations per the tool list.
sop_steps.hint: Tool numbers in the program must match physical tool station numbers.

sop_steps.instruction: Set work offsets (G54) by touching off the part datum.
sop_steps.hint: Touch off on the correct datum face — not just any convenient surface.

sop_steps.instruction: Set tool length/diameter offsets for each loaded tool.
Load and verify the correct CNC program matches the job traveler revision.
sop_steps.hint: Running the wrong program revision is a common and costly mistake.

sop_steps.instruction: Run a dry run (air cut, no material, or single-block mode) to verify toolpath clearances.
sop_steps.hint: Watch for tool-to-fixture clearance especially on rapid moves.

sop_steps.instruction: Close and lock the machine enclosure before starting production.

decision_points.prompt: The loaded program is revision C, but the job traveler specifies revision D. What do you do?

options.text: Run it anyway — revisions are usually close enough
options.consequence: Running the wrong revision can scrap the part or damage tooling on unexpected geometry.

options.text: Stop and locate/load revision D before proceeding
options.consequence: Correct — program revision must always match the job traveler exactly.

decision_points.prompt: During the dry run, you notice the toolpath comes within 2mm of the fixture clamp on one pass. What do you do?

options.text: Proceed to production, 2mm is probably fine
options.consequence: Thermal expansion and vibration during real cutting can close that margin and cause a crash.

options.text: Stop, adjust fixture position or program, and re-run the dry run
options.consequence: Correct — tight clearances found in dry run must be resolved before production.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner ran a program revision that didn't match the job traveler.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Risk of scrapped part, tool breakage, or machine crash on unexpected geometry.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner skipped the dry run and went straight to production cutting.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Undetected clearance or offset errors become a live crash risk during production.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner proceeded to production despite a tight clearance found during dry run.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Machine crash risk — potential damage to tooling, fixture, or spindle.

possible_mistakes.description: Work or tool offsets set incorrectly or from the wrong datum.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Part dimensions out of tolerance, or tool-to-part collision.

possible_mistakes.description: Production run started with the machine enclosure open or unlocked.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Direct exposure to moving spindle and flying debris.

hints.text: Touch off on the datum marked with the triangle symbol on the drawing.
Use single-block mode on the first dry run pass to catch issues before full-speed air cutting.

recommendation_rules.reason: Electrical Panel Maintenance reinforces strict sequential procedure-following.
Rebuild foundational equipment/task-matching knowledge before revisiting setup tasks.

simulations.title: Cybersecurity Incident Response
simulations.goal: Detect, contain, and report a suspected security breach on a company workstation while preserving evidence and following the incident-response SLA.

learning_content.what: Cybersecurity Incident Response (IR) is a structured approach to handling security breaches, malware infections, and system compromises. The NIST IR framework defines six phases: Preparation → Detection → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons Learned. The average cost of a data breach is $4.45 million — fast, correct response directly limits this damage.
learning_content.how: On alert: contain first (network isolate the machine without powering it off) → collect volatile evidence (memory snapshot) → investigate (review logs and running processes) → escalate to the IR lead with findings → remediate only after receiving approval → file a full incident report. Never shut down a compromised machine — RAM evidence (running processes, encryption keys, open network connections) is permanently lost on power-off.

sop_steps.instruction: Acknowledge the security alert within SLA.
sop_steps.hint: SLA clock starts the moment the alert fires.

sop_steps.instruction: Isolate the affected machine from the network (do not power off).
sop_steps.hint: Disconnect network access, but keep the machine running to preserve volatile memory evidence.

sop_steps.instruction: Capture a memory/process snapshot before any further action.
sop_steps.hint: This is your only chance to capture volatile evidence.

sop_steps.instruction: Review recent process list and network connection logs for anomalies.
sop_steps.hint: Look for unfamiliar outbound connections or unsigned processes.

sop_steps.instruction: Identify the likely malicious process/file based on log evidence.
Escalate to the incident response lead with a summary of findings.
sop_steps.hint: Include what was found, when, and containment actions already taken.

sop_steps.instruction: Begin remediation only after escalation is acknowledged.
File the incident report documenting timeline and evidence chain.

decision_points.prompt: You suspect active malware. What is your first containment action?

options.text: Power off the machine immediately
options.consequence: Powering off destroys volatile memory evidence needed for investigation.

options.text: Disconnect the machine from the network but leave it running
options.consequence: Correct — this contains the threat while preserving evidence.

options.text: Ignore it and keep monitoring for now
options.consequence: Delaying containment allows the threat to spread or exfiltrate more data.

decision_points.prompt: You've identified the malicious process. Do you remediate immediately or escalate first?

options.text: Kill the process and delete the file right away
options.consequence: Acting without escalation can destroy evidence needed for a full investigation and bypasses required sign-off.

options.text: Escalate to the incident response lead first, then remediate on approval
options.consequence: Correct — escalation ensures proper evidence handling and coordinated response.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner powered off a compromised machine instead of isolating it.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Loss of volatile memory evidence (running processes, open connections, encryption keys in RAM).

possible_mistakes.description: Learner delayed containment action after detecting a likely active threat.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Extended dwell time allows lateral movement or data exfiltration.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner remediated the threat without escalating to the response lead first.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Bypasses required sign-off and can destroy evidence needed for full investigation or legal follow-up.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner skipped capturing a memory/process snapshot before taking further action.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Volatile evidence is lost permanently once the system state changes.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner did not complete the response within the incident SLA window.
possible_mistakes.consequence: SLA breaches have real contractual and regulatory consequences in industry settings.

hints.text: Isolation = network disconnect, not shutdown. Keep it running.
A good escalation summary answers: what, when, impact so far, actions taken.

recommendation_rules.reason: CNC Setup builds structured diagnostic thinking (clearance/offset troubleshooting) transferable to investigative tasks.
Electrical Panel Maintenance also scores coordination in group lockout scenarios.

simulations.title: Electrical Panel Maintenance
simulations.goal: Safely isolate, inspect, and service a live electrical panel following lockout/verification procedure.

learning_content.what: Electrical panel maintenance involves the inspection, testing, and service of circuit breakers, busbars, and distribution equipment. Live electrical work is one of the highest-risk industrial tasks, capable of causing arc flash, electrocution, and fire. Arc flash can release energy equivalent to a small explosion in milliseconds.
learning_content.how: Always de-energize the panel section under maintenance and verify with a voltmeter before touching anything. Use PPE rated for the arc flash incident energy boundary. Test each breaker by operating it through its full range. Check and re-torque all terminations against specification. Document every finding — a loose terminal that passes today becomes a fire next month.

sop_steps.instruction: Notify affected personnel before beginning isolation.
sop_steps.hint: A quick radio call or posted notice satisfies this.

sop_steps.instruction: Identify the correct circuit breaker for the panel being serviced.
sop_steps.hint: Cross-check the panel schedule label against the work order.

sop_steps.instruction: Switch off the identified breaker.
Apply lock and tag to the breaker with your ID.
sop_steps.hint: Your tag must include name, date, and reason for lockout.

sop_steps.instruction: Test for zero energy using a voltage tester on all phases.
sop_steps.hint: Test the tester itself on a known live source first, then the panel, then the tester again.

sop_steps.instruction: Open the panel cover and visually inspect wiring and terminals.
sop_steps.hint: Look for discoloration, loose terminals, or insulation damage.

sop_steps.instruction: Perform the required maintenance task (e.g. tighten terminal, replace component).
Close the panel cover and remove lock/tag only after confirming work is complete.
sop_steps.hint: Never remove your lock while someone else's is still on the same breaker.

sop_steps.instruction: Restore power and confirm normal operation.

decision_points.prompt: Your voltage tester reads zero on the first try, but you didn't verify the tester on a known live source beforehand. What do you do?

options.text: Proceed — zero reading means it's safe
options.consequence: A faulty tester reading zero can falsely indicate a de-energized circuit.

options.text: Test the tester on a known live source, then re-test the panel
options.consequence: Correct — this is the only way to confirm the tester itself works.

decision_points.prompt: While inspecting, you notice a second person's lock is already on this same breaker from an earlier shift. What do you do?

options.text: Continue your work, it's not your lock so it doesn't matter
options.consequence: Multiple locks indicate multiple people working on this circuit — coordination is required.

options.text: Pause and coordinate with the other technician before proceeding
options.consequence: Correct — group lockout situations require coordination to avoid re-energizing while someone else is still working.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner skipped applying lock/tag before working on the panel.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Panel could be re-energized by another worker while being serviced — risk of severe injury.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner trusted a zero-energy reading without first verifying the tester works.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Arc flash / electrocution risk from a false zero-energy reading.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner ignored evidence of a coexisting lockout by another technician.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Risk of premature re-energization while a co-worker is still exposed.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner isolated the wrong circuit breaker.
possible_mistakes.consequence: The panel being worked on remains live — direct electrocution risk.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner did not complete isolation procedure within the allotted time.
possible_mistakes.consequence: In a real setting, prolonged isolation delays extend production downtime and exposure window.

hints.text: Remember the three-step test: live source, panel, live source again.
Your tag needs name, date, and reason — missing any one is incomplete.

recommendation_rules.reason: Reinforce foundational safety-check habits before returning to safety-critical procedures.
Cybersecurity Incident Response also scores coordination and escalation communication.

simulations.title: End-of-Day Resource Shutdown Procedure
simulations.goal: Safely identify and terminate all non-essential development resources at end-of-day without impacting production systems.

learning_content.what: End-of-day resource management is an operational discipline that prevents unnecessary cloud compute cost while protecting production systems from accidental interference. In cloud environments, idle development and staging resources can represent 30–40% of monthly infrastructure spend if not shut down after hours.
learning_content.how: Always cross-reference any resource you plan to stop against an approved production services list before acting. Use `docker stop` (SIGTERM) rather than `docker kill` for graceful shutdown. Communicate the planned shutdown to the team beforehand. Log every action with a timestamp and your name. When in doubt about a resource — especially if its name contains 'prod' — escalate to a senior engineer rather than guess.

sop_steps.instruction: Check the environment manifest or tagging system to understand what is running in this environment.
sop_steps.hint: Look for an `env-manifest.yaml` or read resource tags in the infrastructure console.

sop_steps.instruction: List all running Docker containers with `docker ps` and identify which ones are tagged as 'dev' or 'staging'.
sop_steps.hint: Container names and labels tell you their role. Look for 'dev', 'staging', 'test' in the name.

sop_steps.instruction: List all running system processes with `ps aux` or `htop` and identify non-essential background jobs.
sop_steps.hint: Look for process names like 'data_sync', 'report_gen' or 'benchmark_runner' that may be development tasks.

sop_steps.instruction: Cross-reference identified processes against the approved 'always-on' production services list.
sop_steps.hint: The approved production services list is at /etc/skilltrack/prod-services.txt. Any service NOT on the list is fair game to stop.

sop_steps.instruction: Stop identified development databases (redis-dev, postgres-staging) using `docker stop` gracefully.
sop_steps.hint: Use `docker stop <container>` rather than `docker kill` — it sends SIGTERM first for clean shutdown.

sop_steps.instruction: Terminate identified non-essential background jobs using `kill <PID>` (SIGTERM, not SIGKILL).
sop_steps.hint: SIGTERM allows the process to save state. Only use SIGKILL (kill -9) if SIGTERM doesn't work.

sop_steps.instruction: Verify that all production services are still running correctly after your changes.
sop_steps.hint: Re-run `docker ps` and check that production containers (labeled 'prod') are still up and healthy.

sop_steps.instruction: Log the shutdown activity: what was stopped, by whom, and at what time — in the team's ops log.
sop_steps.hint: This log is critical if a production issue is discovered overnight that traces back to what you shut down.

decision_points.prompt: You see a process named `data_sync_job_prod` consuming high CPU. It is not in the team's approved list. Do you kill it?

options.text: Yes — it's not on the approved list so it should be stopped.
options.consequence: The 'prod' suffix in the name indicates it is a production job. Killing it causes a production data sync failure.

options.text: No — the 'prod' label is a red flag. Escalate to a senior engineer before touching it.
options.consequence: Correct. When in doubt about a production resource, always escalate rather than act unilaterally.

decision_points.prompt: After stopping postgres-staging, a co-worker messages you saying they needed that database for an overnight batch job. What do you do?

options.text: Apologise and say they should have told me.
options.consequence: Blaming others is not productive. Your EOD process should include communicating the shutdown to the team.

options.text: Restart postgres-staging immediately and update the EOD process to notify the team next time.
options.consequence: Correct. Restore the required resource and improve the process to prevent this in future.

possible_mistakes.description: Terminated a production resource without authorization.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Causes production data loss or outage.

possible_mistakes.description: Left development/staging resources running unnecessarily.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Wasted cloud compute costs and potential licensing violations.

possible_mistakes.description: Shut down resources without notifying the team.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Unexpected downtime for colleagues who needed those resources.

possible_mistakes.description: Did not log what was shut down.
possible_mistakes.consequence: No audit trail if a production issue arises overnight and root-cause analysis is needed.

hints.text: Run `docker ps --filter name=dev` to filter only development containers.
If a process name contains 'prod', 'prd', or 'production' — treat it as a production resource.

simulations.title: Industrial Pump Equipment Assembly
simulations.goal: Correctly assemble a modular centrifugal pump housing to manufacturing specification with correct part orientation and torque sequence.

learning_content.what: Industrial equipment assembly requires strict adherence to Bills of Materials, torque specifications, and installation sequences. A centrifugal pump with a reversed impeller generates zero flow. One with an under-torqued gasket leaks under pressure. Precision assembly is a quality-critical task where a single error can result in catastrophic failure during operation.
learning_content.how: Always verify all parts against the BOM before starting. Inspect mating surfaces for burrs or damage. Lubricate seals only with the approved compound (wrong lubricant degrades elastomers). Install rotating parts in the correct orientation by following the flow direction arrow. Torque fasteners in a three-pass star pattern (30% → 70% → 100%). Perform a hand-rotation check after assembly — any drag means something is wrong.

sop_steps.instruction: Retrieve and verify all assembly components against the Bill of Materials (BOM) for part numbers and quantities.
sop_steps.hint: Check each component's part number label against the BOM. A single wrong part can cause pump failure.

sop_steps.instruction: Inspect the pump housing bore for debris, surface damage, and dimensional compliance.
sop_steps.hint: Wipe the bore with a clean lint-free cloth. Any scoring or burr must be deburred before assembly.

sop_steps.instruction: Place the base gasket onto the pump housing, ensuring all bolt holes are aligned.
sop_steps.hint: The gasket has a notch on one edge that aligns with the housing orientation pin.

sop_steps.instruction: Apply a thin, even coat of assembly lubricant to the impeller shaft seal.
sop_steps.hint: Use only the approved silicone grease. Never use petroleum-based grease on elastomer seals.

sop_steps.instruction: Insert the impeller into the housing with the curved blades facing upward (toward the outlet port).
sop_steps.hint: Identify the outlet port on the housing — the impeller blades must curve toward it for correct flow.

sop_steps.instruction: Position the top cover and hand-tighten all bolts before applying torque.
sop_steps.hint: All bolts must be hand-tight before any are torqued. This ensures even seating of the gasket.

sop_steps.instruction: Torque all bolts to the specified value (35 Nm) in a star pattern using a calibrated torque wrench.
sop_steps.hint: A star pattern means tightening bolts across from each other — never in a circle. Do 3 passes: 30%, 70%, 100%.

sop_steps.instruction: Rotate the shaft by hand to confirm it turns freely without binding or dragging.
sop_steps.hint: Any resistance or roughness during hand-rotation means something is misaligned or incorrectly installed.

decision_points.prompt: You accidentally dropped the impeller during installation. It appears undamaged visually. What do you do?

options.text: Wipe it off and install it — it looks fine.
options.consequence: Micro-fractures not visible to the eye can propagate under operational stress and cause catastrophic failure.

options.text: Tag the impeller as 'Dropped — inspect required' and request a replacement.
options.consequence: Correct. Precision rotating parts that have been dropped must be re-certified before installation.

decision_points.prompt: The shaft rotates but feels slightly rough in one spot during hand-rotation. What do you do?

options.text: It's minor — install the pump and run it to see if the roughness goes away.
options.consequence: Running a pump with internal friction damage will rapidly accelerate seal and bearing failure.

options.text: Disassemble, inspect for the source of drag, and correct before reassembling.
options.consequence: Correct. Any rotational drag must be found and resolved before commissioning.

possible_mistakes.description: Installed a precision component that was dropped without re-inspection.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Catastrophic pump failure during operation from hidden micro-fracture.

possible_mistakes.description: Installed the impeller with the blades facing the wrong direction.
possible_mistakes.consequence: The pump will generate no flow and may create destructive pressure oscillations.

possible_mistakes.description: Tightened bolts in a circular (spiral) pattern instead of a star pattern.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Uneven gasket compression causes leaks and early gasket failure.

possible_mistakes.description: Commissioned pump without resolving rotational drag found during hand-rotation check.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Rapid bearing and seal destruction leading to pump failure.

possible_mistakes.description: Assembled pump without verifying parts against the Bill of Materials.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Wrong part numbers may result in dimensional mismatches or incompatible materials.

hints.text: Star torque pattern: tighten the bolt directly opposite each one you just tightened.
The outlet port is the larger diameter port on the top of the housing casing.

simulations.title: Fire Emergency Response
simulations.goal: Detect, report, safely evacuate and account for all personnel during a simulated workplace fire.

learning_content.what: Fire emergency response is a structured set of actions from initial detection through to full evacuation and personnel accountability. Smoke inhalation — not burns — is responsible for the majority of fire fatalities, making route selection and acting quickly the top priorities.
learning_content.how: Follow RACE: Remove people from danger, Alarm (pull station), Contain (close fire doors), Evacuate/Extinguish. Only attempt to extinguish small, contained fires using the PASS technique (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep). Always feel a door before opening it — a hot door means fire is on the other side. Stay low in smoke. Always report to the assembly point for headcount.

sop_steps.instruction: Identify the fire source and confirm it is not a false alarm.
sop_steps.hint: Look for visible flames, smoke, or a burning smell before proceeding.

sop_steps.instruction: Activate the nearest fire alarm pull station immediately.
sop_steps.hint: Pull the alarm before attempting to fight the fire or alerting others verbally.

sop_steps.instruction: Call emergency services (fire brigade / 101) and report location and fire size.
sop_steps.hint: State your building name, floor, and the approximate fire size.

sop_steps.instruction: Assess fire size — only attempt extinguisher use if the fire is smaller than a wastebasket.
sop_steps.hint: PASS technique: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep. If unsure, evacuate immediately.

sop_steps.instruction: Alert nearby colleagues verbally and begin guiding them toward the exit.
sop_steps.hint: Shout 'FIRE! Evacuate now!' and direct them to follow you. Do not wait for stragglers.

sop_steps.instruction: Navigate to the nearest safe fire exit. Feel the door before opening.
sop_steps.hint: If the door is hot to the touch, the corridor beyond is on fire. Use the alternative exit.

sop_steps.instruction: Close all fire doors behind you during evacuation to slow fire spread.
sop_steps.hint: Fire doors are rated to hold back fire for 30–60 minutes. Always close them behind you.

sop_steps.instruction: Report to the designated assembly point and confirm headcount with the fire marshal.
sop_steps.hint: The assembly point is marked on the site map. Do not re-enter the building.

decision_points.prompt: The fire is the size of a large desk. You have an extinguisher. Do you try to fight it?

options.text: Yes, I'll use the extinguisher to fight it.
options.consequence: A desk-sized fire is beyond the scope of a portable extinguisher. Risk of being trapped.

options.text: No, this is too large. Evacuate immediately.
options.consequence: Correct. Only attempt extinguishing small, contained fires where you have a clear escape path.

decision_points.prompt: The primary exit route is blocked by heavy smoke. A secondary exit is visible but further away. What do you do?

options.text: Run through the smoke quickly — it's faster.
options.consequence: Smoke inhalation is the leading cause of fire casualties. Even brief exposure can be fatal.

options.text: Drop low and crawl to the secondary exit.
options.consequence: Correct. Clean air is near the floor. Stay low and take the alternative route.

possible_mistakes.description: Evacuated without pulling the fire alarm.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Others in the building are left unaware of the fire.

possible_mistakes.description: Chose to run through smoke-filled corridor.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Extremely high risk of asphyxiation and loss of orientation.

possible_mistakes.description: Attempted to use a portable extinguisher on a fire too large to control.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Wasted time and risk of being trapped or overcome by the fire.

possible_mistakes.description: Did not report to the assembly point or check in with the fire marshal.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Emergency services may unnecessarily send rescuers back into the building.

possible_mistakes.description: Used the elevator during the fire evacuation.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Elevators can trap occupants if power fails or smoke enters the shaft.

hints.text: If you see smoke coming under the door gap, do NOT open it. Use the secondary exit.
PASS: Pull pin, Aim at base of fire, Squeeze handle, Sweep side to side.

simulations.title: Git & Team Collaboration Workflow
simulations.goal: Successfully merge a feature branch into main while resolving a real merge conflict without losing any teammate's work.

learning_content.what: Git is the de facto standard version control system used by over 90% of development teams worldwide. Merge conflicts arise whenever two people modify the same lines of the same file in different branches. Understanding how to resolve conflicts cleanly — preserving both parties' intent — is a fundamental collaborative development skill.
learning_content.how: Always fetch before merging to get the latest remote state. Use `git log --graph` to understand branch divergence visually. Merge main INTO your feature branch (not the other way). For each conflict, read both the 'ours' and 'theirs' sections carefully before deciding. Remove every conflict marker. Submit small, focused pull requests — a PR with 50+ changed files is a code review antipattern that hides bugs.

sop_steps.instruction: Fetch the latest changes from the origin repository using `git fetch origin`.
sop_steps.hint: `git fetch` downloads remote changes without modifying your local working directory.

sop_steps.instruction: Run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph --all` to understand the current branch divergence.
sop_steps.hint: The graph view shows you visually where your branch and the main branch have diverged.

sop_steps.instruction: Checkout your feature branch and merge the latest main into it to bring it up to date.
sop_steps.hint: Run: `git checkout feature-login` then `git merge origin/main`.

sop_steps.instruction: Run `git status` to identify all files with merge conflicts.
sop_steps.hint: Files with 'both modified' status in git status are the ones with conflicts requiring manual resolution.

sop_steps.instruction: Open each conflicted file, understand both changes, and resolve the conflict by keeping the correct logic.
sop_steps.hint: Remove ALL conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>). The resulting file must be syntactically valid.

sop_steps.instruction: Stage the resolved files with `git add <file>` and verify no conflict markers remain.
sop_steps.hint: Search for '<<<<<<' in the file before staging to ensure all markers are removed.

sop_steps.instruction: Commit the merge with a descriptive commit message explaining what was resolved.
sop_steps.hint: A good merge commit message: 'Merge main into feature-login: resolve auth.js login logic conflict'.

sop_steps.instruction: Push the resolved feature branch to origin and open a Pull Request for team review.
sop_steps.hint: Use `git push origin feature-login`. The PR allows teammates to review before merging to main.

decision_points.prompt: You aren't sure which version of the conflicting code in auth.js is correct — yours or your teammate's. What do you do?

options.text: Keep your version and delete the teammate's code.
options.consequence: Silently overwrites a teammate's feature without understanding it — introduces a likely regression.

options.text: Force push your branch to main to override everything.
options.consequence: Rewrites shared history and destroys your teammate's entire commit history on that branch.

options.text: Contact your teammate, review both changes together, and agree on the correct merged logic.
options.consequence: Correct. Code review and communication are essential when you are unsure about conflicting logic.

decision_points.prompt: Your PR shows 47 changed files across multiple unrelated features. Your teammate asks you to split it. What do you do?

options.text: Insist on merging as-is — splitting is too much extra work.
options.consequence: Large PRs are difficult to review correctly and significantly increase the risk of bugs being merged.

options.text: Agree to split into separate, focused PRs for each feature.
options.consequence: Correct. Small, focused PRs improve review quality and reduce merge risk.

possible_mistakes.description: Used `git push --force` on a shared branch.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Destroys team commit history and may delete colleagues' work permanently.

possible_mistakes.description: Resolved conflict by deleting a teammate's code without understanding it.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Introduced a regression into the codebase silently.

possible_mistakes.description: Committed a file that still contained Git conflict markers.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Syntax errors break the build pipeline for the entire team.

possible_mistakes.description: Submitted an oversized PR with unrelated changes mixed together.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Reduces code review effectiveness and increases the probability of bugs slipping through.

hints.text: Search the file for '<<<<<<<' using Ctrl+F to ensure no conflict markers are left.
Always merge `origin/main` into your feature branch, not the other way around. Keep main clean.

simulations.title: Workplace Hazard Identification
simulations.goal: Systematically survey and report all unsafe conditions and hazards in a factory workspace.

learning_content.what: Hazard identification is the process of recognising workplace conditions that could cause injury or illness. It is the first and most critical step in a risk assessment cycle. Unidentified hazards cannot be controlled — they become incidents waiting to happen.
learning_content.how: Use a zone-by-zone checklist to ensure no area is skipped. Categorise hazards by type: physical (trip, impact), chemical (spill, fume), and safety systems (blocked exits, faulty guards). Rate each hazard by severity and likelihood. Raise immediate corrective actions for critical findings. Log everything — documented hazards can be tracked, corrected, and audited.

sop_steps.instruction: Obtain the area hazard identification checklist before starting the inspection.
sop_steps.hint: The checklist is at the safety station near the area entrance. It organizes your inspection into zones.

sop_steps.instruction: Scan the floor area for slip, trip, and fall hazards including spills, loose cables, and misplaced tools.
sop_steps.hint: Walk the full perimeter first, then check the center. Look for wet floor signs that may be missing.

sop_steps.instruction: Inspect all emergency exits — confirm they are unobstructed, clearly signed, and unlocked.
sop_steps.hint: Any storage, pallets, or equipment blocking the exit path must be immediately removed.

sop_steps.instruction: Inspect all fire extinguishers: verify pressure gauge is in the green zone, pin is intact, and inspection tag is current.
sop_steps.hint: If the inspection tag is more than 12 months old, the extinguisher is overdue for service.

sop_steps.instruction: Inspect all machinery — look for missing safety guards, exposed rotating parts, and warning labels.
sop_steps.hint: All rotating parts (belts, gears, shafts) must be enclosed by a physical guard.

sop_steps.instruction: Check chemical storage area for proper labeling, SDS availability, and segregation of incompatibles.
sop_steps.hint: Flammables and oxidizers must be stored separately. Each container must have an MSDS/SDS sheet accessible.

sop_steps.instruction: Verify adequate lighting in all inspection zones, including emergency lighting units.
sop_steps.hint: Emergency lighting units have a test button. Push it to verify the backup battery activates the lights.

sop_steps.instruction: Record all identified hazards in the incident reporting system with a severity rating and corrective action.
sop_steps.hint: Critical hazards (blocked exits, missing guards) must trigger immediate corrective action, not just a report.

decision_points.prompt: You spot a pallet of boxes temporarily placed in front of a fire exit door. What is your immediate action?

options.text: Note it in the report for the next safety meeting.
options.consequence: A blocked exit is an immediate critical hazard — it cannot wait for a scheduled meeting.

options.text: Immediately move the pallet or call someone to move it now.
options.consequence: Correct. Emergency exits must be clear at all times. This is a critical hazard requiring immediate action.

decision_points.prompt: You find two unlabeled chemical containers stored together. What should you do?

options.text: Assume they are the same chemical and leave them.
options.consequence: Unknown chemicals stored together may be incompatible and cause a violent reaction.

options.text: Segregate the containers and tag them 'Unknown — Do Not Use' until identified.
options.consequence: Correct. Unidentified chemicals must be isolated and reported to the supervisor for identification.

possible_mistakes.description: Failed to take immediate action on a critical hazard (blocked exit).
possible_mistakes.consequence: Leaves the hazard active, endangering all personnel in the area.

possible_mistakes.description: Failed to identify a clearly visible hazard during the inspection.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Unidentified hazards remain active and lead to future incidents.

possible_mistakes.description: Ignored unlabeled chemical containers.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Incompatible chemicals stored together can cause fire, explosion, or toxic gas release.

possible_mistakes.description: Completed inspection without logging any findings.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Hazards that are not documented cannot be tracked, corrected, or audited.

hints.text: Pay close attention to floor areas near chemical storage — spills may not be visible from a distance.
The green zone on a fire extinguisher pressure gauge is between the two red lines.

simulations.title: Hydraulic/Pneumatic System Diagnosis
simulations.goal: Diagnose pressure drops and flow restrictions in a fluid power network using systematic isolation and Darcy-Weisbach analysis.

learning_content.what: Hydraulic systems transmit force using pressurised fluid. Faults manifest as pressure drops, sluggish actuators, overheating oil, or excessive noise. The Darcy-Weisbach equation governs pressure loss in fluid lines, meaning leaks, blockages, and worn valve seats all create measurable signatures at system gauges that can be traced systematically.
learning_content.how: Begin diagnosis at the pump (the highest-pressure point) and work downstream. Use systematic branch isolation: close one branch at a time with isolation valves and observe system pressure response. A pressure rise indicates flow was leaving through that branch. A flow meter quantifies internal leakage through worn seals. Always consult the hydraulic schematic before touching any valve — the wrong valve closed at the wrong time can cause a dangerous pressure spike.

sop_steps.instruction: Review the hydraulic schematic to understand the circuit topology (pump, valves, actuator, relief valve locations).
sop_steps.hint: Identify Pump P1, Branch A (Valve V1 → Actuator A1), Branch B (Valve V2 → Actuator A2), and the main relief valve RV1.

sop_steps.instruction: Check the system at rest: verify reservoir oil level and pump case drain temperature.
sop_steps.hint: Low oil level causes cavitation. Case drain temperature above 70°C indicates pump wear.

sop_steps.instruction: Run the system and record the main pump output pressure at gauge G1.
sop_steps.hint: The system should rest at 3000 PSI (207 bar). Significant deviation indicates a fault.

sop_steps.instruction: Record actuator A1 and A2 operating pressures under normal load at gauges G2 and G3.
sop_steps.hint: Normal actuator pressure should be 10–15% below pump pressure due to line losses.

sop_steps.instruction: Isolate Branch A by closing Valve V1 and observe how system pressure responds.
sop_steps.hint: If pressure rises when V1 is closed, Branch A was consuming flow — it is the source of the pressure drop.

sop_steps.instruction: With V1 closed, observe Actuator A2 pressure at G3 to isolate Branch B performance.
sop_steps.hint: If Branch B pressure also drops now, the fault is upstream of both branches (pump or relief valve).

sop_steps.instruction: Perform a flow meter test across each suspected component to quantify internal leakage.
sop_steps.hint: A flow meter shows if more fluid is going in than coming out — the difference is internal leakage through worn seals.

sop_steps.instruction: Based on all readings, identify the root cause, record findings, and tag the faulty component for repair.
sop_steps.hint: Use a logic fault tree: is the fault upstream (pump/relief) or downstream (valves/actuators)?

decision_points.prompt: Closing V1 causes system pressure to spike above the relief valve setting of 3300 PSI. What does this indicate?

options.text: The relief valve RV1 is stuck closed and not relieving pressure.
options.consequence: The relief valve IS operating — it is venting the excess pressure. If it were stuck, pressure would keep rising.

options.text: Branch B is completely blocked (deadhead), forcing all pump flow over the relief valve.
options.consequence: Correct. Closing V1 and finding no flow path causes a deadhead — the pump recirculates entirely through RV1.

decision_points.prompt: The pump pressure gauge reads only 1800 PSI at rest instead of 3000 PSI. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Relief valve is stuck open, bleeding pressure back to tank.
options.consequence: Correct. A stuck-open relief valve is the most common cause of low system pressure at rest.

options.text: The pressure gauge is faulty.
options.consequence: Possible, but gauge failure should be confirmed by cross-referencing with a second gauge before replacing the relief valve.

possible_mistakes.description: Misidentified the hydraulic system behaviour, leading to the wrong component diagnosis.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Replacing the wrong component wastes time, money, and leaves the real fault unresolved.

possible_mistakes.description: Attempted diagnosis without systematically isolating branches.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Readings in a parallel circuit are inconclusive without isolation, leading to misdiagnosis.

possible_mistakes.description: Assumed gauge failure without cross-verifying with a second gauge or transducer.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Leads to replacing a functional gauge while the actual fault (relief valve) remains.

possible_mistakes.description: Began diagnosis without reviewing the hydraulic schematic.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Risk of misidentifying circuit topology and closing the wrong valves.

hints.text: Turn the valve handle perpendicular to the pipe direction to close it.
Always record baseline pressures BEFORE isolating any branches — you need a reference point.

simulations.title: Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) Procedure
simulations.goal: Safely isolate ALL hazardous energy sources before maintenance to prevent accidental machine startup.

learning_content.what: Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) is an OSHA-mandated safety procedure that prevents the accidental energization of machinery during maintenance. Each year, failure to implement LOTO correctly causes over 120 fatalities and 50,000 injuries in industrial settings globally. It applies to all energy forms: electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, thermal, mechanical, and gravitational.
learning_content.how: Follow six steps strictly in order: Notify personnel → Shut down the machine normally → Isolate ALL energy sources (not just electrical) → Apply your personal padlock → Attach a filled-out tag → Verify zero energy (start attempt + voltmeter probe). Every individual worker performing maintenance must apply their own personal padlock. Never share a key.

sop_steps.instruction: Review the machine-specific LOTO procedure sheet for this equipment.
sop_steps.hint: The LOTO procedure sheet is posted on the machine panel. It lists every energy source.

sop_steps.instruction: Notify all affected personnel that the machine will be shut down.
sop_steps.hint: Verbal notification and a posted sign on the machine are both required.

sop_steps.instruction: Shut down the equipment using its normal stopping procedure.
sop_steps.hint: Use the control panel OFF button — do not trip the breaker as the first step.

sop_steps.instruction: Isolate the main power breaker by flipping it to the OFF position.
sop_steps.hint: The main breaker is in the motor control center (MCC). Flip it to the OFF position.

sop_steps.instruction: Apply the physical safety padlock to the breaker hasp.
sop_steps.hint: Each worker must apply their own personal padlock. Never share a key.

sop_steps.instruction: Attach the LOTO warning tag to the padlock, filled out with your name, date and reason.
sop_steps.hint: A tag without a name and date is invalid and does not count as a proper tagout.

sop_steps.instruction: Dissipate or restrain any stored energy (de-energize capacitors, bleed pneumatic lines, block gravity-held parts).
sop_steps.hint: After cutting power, check for pneumatic air lines, springs, gravity loads, and capacitor banks.

sop_steps.instruction: Verify zero energy state: attempt to start the machine, then use a voltmeter on all isolation points.
sop_steps.hint: First press the START button to prove the machine won't start, then probe with the voltmeter. Both checks are required.

decision_points.prompt: You notice a secondary pneumatic air line connected to the machine. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore it — the electrical breaker is enough.
options.consequence: Stored pneumatic energy can still cause mechanical movement and injury.

options.text: Close the pneumatic shutoff valve and apply a valve lockout device.
options.consequence: Correct. All energy sources — electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic — must be isolated.

decision_points.prompt: The voltmeter still reads 6V at the load side of the breaker. Do you proceed with maintenance?

options.text: Yes — 6V is too small to be dangerous.
options.consequence: Any residual voltage must be investigated. It may indicate a faulty isolation or a secondary feed.

options.text: No — stop and investigate the source of the residual voltage.
options.consequence: Correct. Zero energy verification must be confirmed. Residual voltage must be traced and resolved.

possible_mistakes.description: Applied tag without a physical padlock.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Tags are only warnings — they do not physically prevent re-energization.

possible_mistakes.description: Failed to isolate a secondary energy source (pneumatic, hydraulic, or gravity).
possible_mistakes.consequence: Stored energy can release unexpectedly causing serious injury.

possible_mistakes.description: Proceeded with maintenance despite a non-zero voltmeter reading.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Worker exposed to live electrical energy.

possible_mistakes.description: Failed to notify affected personnel before shutting down equipment.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Co-workers may be unexpectedly affected by the shutdown.

possible_mistakes.description: Used a shared or master padlock key instead of a personal lock.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Another worker could re-energize the machine while maintenance is in progress.

hints.text: Remember: Lock OUT first, then Tag OUT. Never tag without locking.
Stored energy includes springs, suspended loads, pressure lines, and charged capacitors.

recommendation_rules.reason: Review basic electrical safety and hazard awareness before attempting LOTO on real equipment.

simulations.title: Three-Phase Induction Motor Troubleshooting
simulations.goal: Systematically diagnose a three-phase induction motor fault using electrical measurements and logical fault isolation.

learning_content.what: Three-phase induction motors are the workhorse of industrial production, accounting for over 70% of industrial electricity consumption. They are reliable but fail from electrical faults (single-phasing, insulation breakdown, overloading) or mechanical faults (bearing wear, rotor bar damage). Misdiagnosis leads to replacing functional components while the real fault remains.
learning_content.how: Use a structured diagnostic sequence: nameplate review → visual inspection → insulation resistance (megger test) → supply voltage balance → running current balance → thermal imaging. Always apply LOTO before any physical inspection or megger test. Compare all readings against the nameplate rated values. Zero current on one phase is single-phasing — the most dangerous and most common fault.

sop_steps.instruction: Review the motor nameplate data: rated voltage, rated current (FLA), power factor and insulation class.
sop_steps.hint: The nameplate is on the motor housing. Note the Full Load Amps — this is your reference for current measurements.

sop_steps.instruction: Apply LOTO on the motor disconnect before performing any physical inspection.
sop_steps.hint: Never open the terminal box or touch windings without locking out and verifying zero energy.

sop_steps.instruction: Perform a visual inspection: check for burn marks, oil contamination, and bearing condition.
sop_steps.hint: Discoloration or a burning smell near the windings indicates overheating. Check the shaft for excessive play.

sop_steps.instruction: Perform an insulation resistance test (megger) between each winding phase and ground.
sop_steps.hint: LOTO must be applied before megger testing. A reading below 1 MΩ indicates insulation breakdown.

sop_steps.instruction: Remove LOTO, restore power, and measure line-to-line voltages at the motor terminals (L1-L2, L2-L3, L3-L1).
sop_steps.hint: All three readings should be within 1% of each other (e.g. 480V ± 5V). Imbalance suggests supply issue.

sop_steps.instruction: Clamp-meter all three phases while motor is running under normal load and record L1, L2, L3 currents.
sop_steps.hint: Current imbalance exceeding 10% between phases is significant. Zero current on one phase = single-phasing.

sop_steps.instruction: Measure motor casing temperature using a thermal gun. Compare against the rated temperature rise.
sop_steps.hint: Point the thermal gun at the motor casing (not the cooling fins). Overtemperature suggests blocked ventilation or overloading.

sop_steps.instruction: Based on all measurements, identify the fault and document findings for the maintenance log.
sop_steps.hint: Use all gathered data to narrow the fault to a single root cause before ordering parts or repairs.

decision_points.prompt: Your readings are: L1=10A, L2=10A, L3=0A. The motor hums but does not rotate. What is the fault?

options.text: Motor is overloaded.
options.consequence: Overloading draws HIGH current on all three phases, not zero on one.

options.text: Single-phasing — loss of Phase 3 supply.
options.consequence: Correct. The motor lost one phase, causing the humming and failure to start.

options.text: Bearing failure.
options.consequence: Bearing failure causes mechanical noise and draws high current on all phases, not zero on one.

decision_points.prompt: Megger test shows 0.5 MΩ insulation resistance on Phase 2 winding. What action do you take?

options.text: Put the motor back into service — 0.5 MΩ is still some resistance.
options.consequence: Below 1 MΩ indicates imminent winding failure. Running this motor risks catastrophic failure.

options.text: Tag the motor as failed, remove from service, and schedule rewinding.
options.consequence: Correct. Failed insulation must be addressed before the motor is run again.

possible_mistakes.description: Incorrectly diagnosed the motor fault from current readings.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Leads to unnecessary replacement of functional parts and wasted downtime.

possible_mistakes.description: Attempted to use megger without applying LOTO first.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Destroys the test instrument and causes a severe electrical arc flash hazard.

possible_mistakes.description: Returned motor to service with failed insulation resistance.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Winding failure causes fire risk and unplanned shutdown.

possible_mistakes.description: Made current measurements without checking the rated FLA on the nameplate.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Cannot determine if measured current is abnormal without a reference value.

hints.text: A megger reading below 1 MΩ to ground indicates insulation breakdown.
Clamp the meter jaws around a single cable, not around the conduit.

recommendation_rules.reason: Reinforce energy isolation rules before performing live electrical measurements.

simulations.title: PPE Compliance & Inspection
simulations.goal: Select, inspect, and correctly wear the appropriate personal protective equipment before entering a hazard zone.

learning_content.what: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is any device or garment worn to minimise exposure to workplace hazards. Employers must assess risks and provide appropriate PPE free of charge under health and safety regulations. PPE is the last line of defence — it does not eliminate the hazard, it only reduces risk.
learning_content.how: Select PPE based on the specific hazard type (chemical, impact, heat). Inspect every item before use for cracks, tears, or expiry. Wear in the correct sequence to ensure seals and closures work properly. Never use damaged PPE — replace it immediately. Always confirm at the compliance checkpoint before entering a hazard zone.

sop_steps.instruction: Identify the hazard zone and required PPE category from the posted signage.
sop_steps.hint: Check the hazard sign at the zone entrance — it lists required PPE.

sop_steps.instruction: Select safety helmet from the PPE rack.
sop_steps.hint: Helmets are color-coded by role; pick the one matching your assigned role.

sop_steps.instruction: Inspect helmet for cracks or damage before wearing.
sop_steps.hint: Look for hairline cracks near the shell edge and check the strap.

sop_steps.instruction: Select and inspect safety goggles.
sop_steps.hint: Goggles should have no scratches obstructing vision.

sop_steps.instruction: Select and inspect gloves rated for the task.
sop_steps.hint: Match glove rating (cut/chemical/heat) to the task on the signage.

sop_steps.instruction: Select safety footwear and verify sole condition.
sop_steps.hint: Steel-toe boots with intact soles are required in this zone.

sop_steps.instruction: Don all selected PPE and verify fit (straps, seals, closures).
sop_steps.hint: A loose chinstrap or gaping goggle seal counts as improper fit.

sop_steps.instruction: Confirm compliance at the checkpoint scanner before entry.
sop_steps.hint: The scanner checks that all required PPE items are logged as worn.

decision_points.prompt: The helmet you picked has a small hairline crack near the rim. What do you do?

options.text: Wear it anyway, the crack looks minor
options.consequence: A compromised helmet fails to protect against impact.

options.text: Discard it and select a replacement helmet
options.consequence: Correct — damaged PPE must never be worn.

options.text: Tape over the crack and wear it
options.consequence: Tape does not restore structural integrity.

decision_points.prompt: The task involves handling a mild solvent, but only cut-resistant gloves are on the rack in your size. What do you do?

options.text: Use the cut-resistant gloves since they're the closest fit
options.consequence: Cut-resistant gloves do not protect against chemical exposure.

options.text: Request chemical-rated gloves from the supervisor before proceeding
options.consequence: Correct — task-appropriate PPE rating must always be matched.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner wore PPE without inspecting it first.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Undetected damage in PPE eliminates its protective function.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner chose to wear or repair damaged PPE instead of replacing it.
possible_mistakes.consequence: A cracked helmet can fail completely on impact.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner selected PPE not rated for the actual task hazard.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Exposure risk specific to the hazard (chemical, thermal, etc.) is not mitigated.

possible_mistakes.description: PPE worn without verifying straps, seals, or closures.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Ill-fitted PPE can shift or fail during actual hazard exposure.

possible_mistakes.description: PPE items donned in an order that skips logical dependency (e.g. gloves before sleeve seals).
possible_mistakes.consequence: Minor procedural inefficiency, not typically hazardous on its own.

hints.text: Always run your thumb along helmet edges to feel for cracks, not just look.
Glove rating labels are printed on the cuff.

recommendation_rules.reason: Electrical Panel Maintenance reinforces safety-critical sequencing and consequence awareness.
CNC Setup builds task-specific equipment knowledge through guided configuration.

simulations.title: Preventive Machine Maintenance
simulations.goal: Complete a full preventive maintenance schedule on a production conveyor machine to detect wear and prevent failure.

learning_content.what: Preventive Maintenance (PM) is a scheduled strategy of inspecting and servicing equipment before failure occurs. Studies show PM reduces unplanned downtime by up to 45% and extends equipment life significantly compared to reactive breakdown maintenance. PM follows a fixed schedule based on time, cycles, or condition readings.
learning_content.how: Execute PM from a standardised checklist covering mechanical, electrical, and safety elements in sequence. Record all measurements (temperatures, oil levels, vibration) against known baseline values. Any out-of-spec reading triggers an immediate decision: correct on the spot or raise a corrective work order before returning the machine to service. Never skip a checklist item without a documented justification.

sop_steps.instruction: Review the preventive maintenance schedule and retrieve the machine's maintenance history log.
sop_steps.hint: The PM schedule shows which components are due for inspection and which were flagged in the last service.

sop_steps.instruction: Inspect the conveyor belt for fraying, edge damage, mis-tracking, and tension.
sop_steps.hint: Check both the carry side and return side. Fraying at the edges often indicates mis-tracking.

sop_steps.instruction: Check all drive chain and sprocket assemblies for wear, elongation, and adequate lubrication.
sop_steps.hint: A worn chain will show 'pitch elongation' — the chain will sag between sprockets more than usual.

sop_steps.instruction: Check lubrication levels in the main gearbox and bearing housings. Top up if below MIN line.
sop_steps.hint: Use the sight glass or dipstick. Only use the manufacturer-specified oil grade — do not mix types.

sop_steps.instruction: Inspect all electrical connections and control panel for loose terminals, corrosion, and heat damage.
sop_steps.hint: Discolored terminals or a burning smell indicate overheating at a connection point.

sop_steps.instruction: Measure motor operating temperature with a thermal imager while machine is running under load.
sop_steps.hint: Aim the thermal gun at the motor casing, not the cooling fins. Normal operating temp is below 80°C.

sop_steps.instruction: Test all safety interlocks, emergency stops, and guarding switches for correct operation.
sop_steps.hint: Each E-stop must stop the machine within 1 second of activation. A slow stop is a failed interlock.

sop_steps.instruction: Record all readings and findings in the maintenance log and schedule corrective actions for any issues found.
sop_steps.hint: Note both pass and fail results — a record of passing inspections is just as important for traceability.

decision_points.prompt: The motor temperature reads 95°C — 15°C above the normal operating range. What is your next step?

options.text: Log the reading and continue the rest of the inspection.
options.consequence: Ignoring an overheating motor can lead to winding failure and a catastrophic unplanned shutdown.

options.text: Initiate a controlled shutdown and investigate the cause before continuing.
options.consequence: Correct. Abnormal temperature readings require immediate investigation to prevent equipment damage.

decision_points.prompt: One of the E-stop buttons activates but the machine takes 4 seconds to stop instead of the required 1 second. What do you do?

options.text: Note it in the log and continue — it still stops eventually.
options.consequence: A slow E-stop is a failed safety interlock. The machine must be taken out of service immediately.

options.text: Take the machine out of service and raise a work order for the interlock system.
options.consequence: Correct. Any safety interlock that does not meet specification must be repaired before the machine is returned to service.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner continued work despite an out-of-spec temperature reading.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Motor continues to overheat and fails, causing unplanned production downtime.

possible_mistakes.description: Failed to take a machine out of service after an E-stop interlock failure.
possible_mistakes.consequence: A worker could be seriously injured if they cannot stop the machine in an emergency.

possible_mistakes.description: Learner skipped a checklist item without justification.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Incomplete preventive maintenance leads to undetected wear and unexpected failures.

possible_mistakes.description: Added incompatible oil type to the gearbox.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Mixed lubricants can degrade and cause accelerated bearing and gear wear.

hints.text: Normal motor operating temperature is below 80°C. Above 90°C is a clear abnormal reading.
A worn chain is safe to measure — use the '3-link elongation' check against manufacturer spec.

recommendation_rules.reason: Motor Troubleshooting provides deeper grounding in motor diagnostics and thermal analysis.

simulations.title: Ubuntu Production Server Management
simulations.goal: Diagnose high CPU load on a production Ubuntu server, identify the failing service, resolve the issue, and document the incident.

learning_content.what: Ubuntu server administration is a core skill for any operations or DevOps engineer. Linux runs the majority of global internet infrastructure. High CPU consumption, failing services, and log analysis are the most common day-to-day operational challenges. Every production incident has a root cause that can be found with the right diagnostic sequence.
learning_content.how: Follow a top-down approach: check system load (uptime) → identify the process (top/htop) → check service status (systemctl) → review journal logs (journalctl) → check resource limits (disk, memory, file descriptors). Always use `systemctl restart` for graceful service recovery. Only use `kill -9` as a last resort when a process is completely unresponsive to SIGTERM.

sop_steps.instruction: Check system uptime and load average using the `uptime` command.
sop_steps.hint: Load average values above your CPU core count indicate sustained overload. E.g. 4.5 on a 4-core system is at limit.

sop_steps.instruction: Run `top` or `htop` and identify the process consuming the most CPU.
sop_steps.hint: In top, press 'P' to sort by CPU usage. Note the process name and PID.

sop_steps.instruction: Check the systemd service status for the identified process using `systemctl status <service>`.
sop_steps.hint: systemctl status will show you if the service is active, failed, or in a restart loop.

sop_steps.instruction: Review the journal logs for the service using `journalctl -u <service> --since '10 min ago'`.
sop_steps.hint: Look for repeated error patterns, infinite loop messages, or OOM (out of memory) kill events.

sop_steps.instruction: Check disk usage with `df -h` and memory usage with `free -m` to rule out resource exhaustion.
sop_steps.hint: A full disk (/var/log or /tmp) can cause services to crash in a loop, creating apparent high CPU.

sop_steps.instruction: Gracefully restart the failing service using `systemctl restart <service>`.
sop_steps.hint: Use `systemctl restart`, not `kill -9`. A graceful restart allows the service to clean up connections.

sop_steps.instruction: Verify the service is running correctly after the restart using `systemctl status` and monitor CPU for 2 minutes.
sop_steps.hint: Watch for the service entering a crash-restart loop — if it fails again within 60 seconds, the root cause is not resolved.

sop_steps.instruction: Document the incident: timestamp, affected service, root cause, action taken, and resolution time.
sop_steps.hint: Log your findings in the incident management system. Even a minor outage requires a brief post-mortem note.

decision_points.prompt: The nginx logs show it is stuck in an infinite redirect loop, consuming 99% CPU. Do you use `kill -9` to force-kill it?

options.text: Yes — kill -9 forces it to stop immediately.
options.consequence: SIGKILL does not allow graceful shutdown, abruptly dropping all active user connections and potentially corrupting state.

options.text: No — use `systemctl restart nginx` for a graceful restart.
options.consequence: Correct. Graceful restarts use SIGTERM first, allowing the service to close connections cleanly.

decision_points.prompt: After restart, nginx fails again within 30 seconds with 'too many open files' error. What do you do?

options.text: Restart it again and hope for the best.
options.consequence: The service will keep failing. Restarting without fixing the root cause is not a resolution.

options.text: Investigate and increase the open file descriptor limit in the service config (LimitNOFILE).
options.consequence: Correct. 'Too many open files' is a kernel ulimit issue. The fix is to raise LimitNOFILE in the systemd service unit.

possible_mistakes.description: Used `kill -9` on a production service unnecessarily.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Abruptly dropped all active client connections and potentially corrupted in-progress request state.

possible_mistakes.description: Restarted the wrong service.
possible_mistakes.consequence: Causes an unrelated production outage while the real high-CPU service remains unresolved.

possible_mistakes.description: Resolved the symptom (restarted service) without investigating the underlying root cause.
possible_mistakes.consequence: The service will fail again, causing recurrent incidents.

possible_mistakes.description: Resolved the incident but did not create any documentation.
possible_mistakes.consequence: No audit trail means the problem cannot be tracked for pattern analysis.

hints.text: If journalctl returns no output for the service, check /var/log/<service>/error.log directly.
Run `lsof | wc -l` to count total open file descriptors system-wide if you suspect a file limit issue.
